prompt: In football, how many points is a field goal worth?
explanation: A field goal is worth 3 points. The ball is kicked through the goalposts above the crossbar, often when a team is close but cannot reach the end zone.
source_notes: NFHS Football Rules Book, scoring section (field goal = 3 points); to verify.

prompt: How many yards long is a football field from one goal line to the other, not counting the end zones?
explanation: It is 100 yards from goal line to goal line. Add the two 10-yard end zones and the whole field is 120 yards long.
source_notes: NFHS Football Rules Book, field diagram and dimensions; to verify.

prompt: In football, what is a safety worth to the defense?
explanation: A safety is worth 2 points. It usually happens when the defense tackles a ball carrier in the offense's own end zone. Then the team that gave up the safety has to kick the ball away, so the defense gets points and the ball.
source_notes: NFHS Football Rules Book, scoring section (safety = 2 points); to verify.

prompt: In football, the offense gets four downs (tries) to gain 10 yards and earn a new first down.
explanation: True! The offense has four downs to move the ball 10 yards. If they make it, they get a fresh set of downs. That is why teams often punt on fourth down.
source_notes: NFHS Football Rules Book, series of downs; to verify.

prompt: How high above the floor is the rim of a regulation basketball hoop?
explanation: The rim is 10 feet above the floor. That height has stayed the same since the game's early days, from high school gyms to the pros.
source_notes: NFHS Basketball Rules Book, court and equipment section (basket height); to verify.

prompt: In basketball, how many points is one made free throw worth?
explanation: Each made free throw is worth 1 point. Free throws are taken from the free-throw line with no defender guarding the shooter, usually after a foul.
source_notes: NFHS Basketball Rules Book, scoring section (free throw = 1 point); to verify.

prompt: How many players does a basketball team have on the court at the same time?
explanation: Each basketball team has 5 players on the court at once. Coaches can swap players in and out during the game.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: In basketball, dribbling the ball with both hands at the same time is allowed.
explanation: False. Dribbling with both hands at once, or stopping and then dribbling again, is a violation often called a double dribble. The other team gets the ball.
source_notes: NFHS Basketball Rules Book, dribble definitions and violations; to verify.

prompt: In rugby, what is it called when a player grounds the ball in the other team's in-goal area to score?
explanation: It is called a try. The player has to press the ball down to the ground over the line, which is how the score got its name.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: What shape is a rugby ball?
explanation: A rugby ball is oval, a bit like a stretched-out egg. That shape makes it bounce in surprising ways.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: In rugby, which way are players allowed to pass the ball with their hands?
explanation: Passes in rugby must go backward or sideways. A pass that travels forward is called a forward pass, and play stops for a scrum. Teams move the ball forward by running and kicking.
source_notes: World Rugby Laws of the Game, definitions and forward pass law; to verify.

prompt: In rugby, a scrum is a way to restart play where players from both teams bind together and push.
explanation: True! In a scrum, the forwards from each team lock together and push while the ball is rolled in between them.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: In indoor volleyball, how many players from each team are on the court at once?
explanation: Each indoor volleyball team has 6 players on the court. Beach volleyball is usually played with just 2 players per side.
source_notes: NFHS Volleyball Rules Book, players and substitutes section; to verify.

prompt: In volleyball, what is the most times a team can hit the ball before it must go over the net (not counting a block)?
explanation: A team gets up to 3 hits to send the ball back over, often a pass, a set and an attack. A touch on a block does not count as one of the three.
source_notes: NFHS Volleyball Rules Book, playing the ball section; to verify.

prompt: In volleyball, what do players use to hit the ball over the net?
explanation: Volleyball players hit the ball with their hands and arms. A bump, a set and a spike are all done without any equipment.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: In volleyball, a team must win a set by at least two points.
explanation: True! A set keeps going until one team leads by two points, even past 25. A close set can finish 26-24, 27-25 or later.
source_notes: NFHS Volleyball Rules Book, scoring and set length section; to verify.

prompt: In soccer, how many players does each team have on the field, including the goalkeeper?
explanation: Each team has 11 players on the field, and one of them is the goalkeeper. Smaller-sided youth games may use fewer.
source_notes: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 3 (the players); NFHS Soccer Rules Book; to verify.

prompt: In soccer, which player is allowed to handle the ball with their hands inside their own penalty area?
explanation: Only the goalkeeper may handle the ball, and only inside their own penalty area. Other field players use their feet, head, chest and thighs. Throw-ins are the one time everyone uses their hands.
source_notes: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 12 (handling the ball); to verify.

prompt: In soccer, what is it called when one player scores three goals in the same game?
explanation: Three goals by one player is a hat trick. A clean sheet means a team did not allow a goal, and the grand slam and triple play come from baseball.
source_notes: General soccer terminology; any standard sports glossary; to verify.

prompt: In soccer, a yellow card from the referee is a warning to a player.
explanation: True! A yellow card is a caution. A red card is more serious and sends the player off the field.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: In baseball, how many balls does a batter need to earn a walk to first base?
explanation: Four balls earns a walk, also called a base on balls. A ball is a pitch outside the strike zone that the batter does not swing at.
source_notes: NFHS Baseball Rules Book, batter and base on balls section; to verify.

prompt: In baseball, how many strikes make a strikeout?
explanation: Three strikes and the batter is out. That is where the saying "three strikes and you're out" comes from.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: In baseball, what do you call a home run hit when the bases are loaded?
explanation: A home run with runners on all three bases is a grand slam. It scores four runs at once, the most possible on a single swing.
source_notes: General baseball terminology; NFHS/MLB glossaries; to verify.

prompt: In baseball, a home run lets the batter run around all the bases and score.
explanation: True! On a home run, the batter rounds first, second and third base and touches home plate to score a run.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: How does a pitcher throw the ball in fastpitch softball?
explanation: Fastpitch softball pitchers throw underhand, often with a windmill arm motion. Even underhand, top pitchers throw very fast from a short distance.
source_notes: NFHS Softball Rules Book, pitching section; to verify.

prompt: In softball, what does the batter use to hit the ball?
explanation: Softball batters swing a bat, just like in baseball.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: In softball, how many outs does the batting team get before the teams switch sides?
explanation: After 3 outs, the teams switch: the fielding team comes in to bat. Baseball works the same way.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: A softball is smaller than a baseball.
explanation: False. A fastpitch softball is bigger, about 12 inches around, while a baseball is about 9 inches around. The "soft" in the name does not mean small!
source_notes: NFHS Softball and Baseball Rules Books, equipment (ball circumference); to verify.

prompt: In wrestling, what is it called when a wrestler holds both of the opponent's shoulders on the mat long enough to end the match?
explanation: That is a fall, often called a pin. It ends the match right away, no matter what the score was.
source_notes: NFHS Wrestling Rules Book, fall definition; to verify.

prompt: What is the padded floor that wrestlers compete on called?
explanation: Wrestlers compete on a thick, padded mat. The padding helps protect them during takedowns.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: Why do wrestlers compete in weight classes?
options: So wrestlers face opponents of similar size
So each team has the same uniforms
So referees can tell wrestlers apart
explanation: Weight classes match wrestlers with opponents close to their own size. That keeps matches fair and lets skill and technique decide the winner.
source_notes: NFHS Wrestling Rules Book, weight classes section; to verify.

prompt: In a wrestling match, each wrestler faces a single opponent.
explanation: True! A wrestling match is one-on-one. In team meets, each match still pits one wrestler against another.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: How long is one lap around the inside lane of a standard outdoor running track?
explanation: One lap of the inside lane is 400 meters. Outer lanes are longer, which is why runners in those lanes start farther ahead in races around the curve.
source_notes: NFHS Track and Field Rules Book; World Athletics track specifications; to verify.

prompt: In a relay race, what do runners pass to their teammates?
explanation: Relay runners pass a baton. The handoff must happen inside a marked exchange zone, so smooth passing can win or lose a race.
source_notes: NFHS Track and Field Rules Book, relay section; to verify.

prompt: How many events are in a decathlon?
explanation: A decathlon has 10 events, held over two days. The word comes from the Greek "deka," meaning ten. The heptathlon has seven events.
source_notes: World Athletics competition rules (combined events); to verify.

prompt: In the long jump, stepping past the takeoff line counts as a foul.
explanation: True! If a jumper's foot goes past the takeoff line, the jump is a foul and does not count. Jumpers practice their run-up so they hit the board just right.
source_notes: NFHS Track and Field Rules Book, long jump section; World Athletics rules; to verify.

prompt: In lacrosse, which player guards the net?
explanation: The goalie guards the net and tries to stop shots, just like a goalkeeper in soccer or a goalie in hockey.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: Lacrosse was first played by which people?
explanation: Lacrosse began with Indigenous peoples of North America, including the Haudenosaunee, centuries ago. Many communities still honor it as an important part of their culture.
source_notes: USA Lacrosse history; Haudenosaunee Nationals history; to verify wording with Content.

prompt: What do lacrosse players use to catch, carry and throw the ball?
options: A stick with a netted head
explanation: Players use a lacrosse stick, sometimes called a crosse. Its netted head, or pocket, lets them catch, cradle and throw the ball.
source_notes: NFHS Boys and Girls Lacrosse Rules Books, equipment section; to verify.

prompt: Lacrosse players can carry the ball in the netted pocket of their stick while running.
explanation: True! Players cradle the ball in the pocket of the stick as they run, then pass or shoot it.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic rules of the game); no expert check needed.

prompt: What is the flat rubber disc used in ice hockey called?
explanation: It is called a puck, and it is made of hard rubber. Pucks are often frozen before games so they slide smoothly and bounce less.
source_notes: USA Hockey Playing Rules, equipment (puck); NFHS Ice Hockey Rules Book; to verify.

prompt: In ice hockey, how many players from each team are on the ice during normal play, including the goalie?
explanation: Each team has 6 players on the ice: a goalie and five skaters. When a player serves a penalty, the team usually plays with one fewer skater.
source_notes: USA Hockey Playing Rules; NFHS Ice Hockey Rules Book, players section; to verify.

prompt: How many periods are in a standard ice hockey game?
explanation: A standard hockey game has three periods. Teams switch ends between periods, and the ice is often resurfaced during the breaks.
source_notes: USA Hockey Playing Rules; NFHS Ice Hockey Rules Book, game length; to verify.

prompt: In ice hockey, a player who gets a penalty sits in the penalty box while their team plays one player short.
explanation: True! The penalized player sits in the penalty box, and their team plays short-handed. The other team gets a power play, a great chance to score.
source_notes: USA Hockey Playing Rules, penalties section; NFHS Ice Hockey Rules Book; to verify.

prompt: In tennis scoring, what does the word "love" mean?
explanation: "Love" means zero in tennis. So a score of 15-love means one player has one point and the other has none.
source_notes: ITF Rules of Tennis, scoring section; to verify.

prompt: In a tennis game, the points go love, 15, 30 and then what?
explanation: After 30 comes 40. One more point after 40 wins the game, as long as the player is at least two points ahead.
source_notes: ITF Rules of Tennis, scoring in a game; to verify.

prompt: In tennis, what is a serve called when the receiver cannot even touch it with their racket?
explanation: That serve is an ace. A let is a serve that clips the net and lands in, so it is replayed, and a fault is a serve that misses the service box.
source_notes: ITF Rules of Tennis and standard tennis glossary; to verify.

prompt: In tennis, when the score in a game is tied at 40-40, it is called deuce.
explanation: True! A 40-40 tie is called deuce. From there, a player must win two points in a row to win the game, first earning "advantage" and then the game.
source_notes: ITF Rules of Tennis, scoring in a game (deuce); to verify.

prompt: What pulls a ball back down to the ground after it is thrown up in the air?
explanation: Gravity pulls everything toward the ground. That is why every pop fly and jump shot comes back down.
source_notes: Common knowledge (basic science); no expert check needed.

prompt: When you exercise hard, you breathe faster mainly to get more of which gas to your muscles?
explanation: Your muscles use oxygen to make energy. Breathing faster brings in more oxygen and also helps your body get rid of carbon dioxide, the gas you breathe out.
source_notes: Introductory biology/physiology texts on respiration during exercise; to verify.

prompt: Why does your body sweat during a game?
options: To cool you down as the sweat dries
To keep your muscles from moving
explanation: Sweat cools you as it evaporates from your skin, carrying heat away from your body. That is why drinking water during practice and games matters.
source_notes: Introductory physiology texts on thermoregulation; to verify.

prompt: If you threw a ball on the Moon as hard as you can on Earth, it would travel farther.
explanation: True! The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's, and there is no air to slow the ball down. An astronaut even hit golf balls on the Moon in 1971.
source_notes: NASA educational material on lunar gravity; Apollo 14 mission history; to verify.

prompt: Rugby is named after a school in a town called Rugby. In which country is it?
explanation: Rugby School is in the town of Rugby, England, where the game's early form developed in the 1800s. Today rugby is loved worldwide, including across the Pacific Islands.
source_notes: World Rugby history; Rugby School history; to verify.

prompt: The ancient Olympic Games began in which country?
explanation: The Olympic Games started in ancient Greece, at a place called Olympia. That is where the name comes from.
source_notes: Common knowledge (world history); no expert check needed.

prompt: Sumo wrestling is a traditional sport from which country?
explanation: Sumo is a traditional sport from Japan. Wrestlers try to push each other out of a ring or make them touch the ground.
source_notes: Common knowledge (world geography and culture); no expert check needed.

prompt: Canada, where ice hockey is hugely popular, is north of the United States.
explanation: True! Canada is directly north of the United States. Hockey is one of the most loved sports there.
source_notes: Common knowledge (world geography); no expert check needed.

prompt: In sports, what does "MVP" stand for?
explanation: MVP stands for Most Valuable Player. It is an honor given to the player who helped their team the most in a game, a tournament or a season.
source_notes: Standard sports glossary; to verify.

prompt: What is a "shutout" in sports?
options: A game stopped because of weather
A game where one team does not score at all
A game that goes into overtime
A game played with no fans
explanation: A shutout is a game where one team keeps the other from scoring at all. It is a big win for the defense and the goalie or pitcher.
source_notes: Standard sports glossary; to verify.

prompt: What do people call it when a team plays a game at its own field or gym?
explanation: A game at your own field or gym is a home game. When a team travels to the other school, it is an away game. A bye week means no game at all.
source_notes: Standard sports glossary; to verify.

prompt: The Olympic flag shows five interlocking rings.
explanation: True! The five rings, in blue, yellow, black, green and red on a white background, stand for the five continents joined together in the Olympic spirit.
source_notes: International Olympic Committee (olympics.com) on the Olympic symbol; to verify.

prompt: The United States government has three branches. Which list names them?
explanation: The three branches are legislative, executive, and judicial. They share the work of making laws, carrying them out, and judging them.
source_notes: National Archives, the Constitution at a glance; to verify.

prompt: The Constitution is the highest law in the United States.
explanation: True! The Constitution sits above other laws in the United States. Public officials promise to support it.
source_notes: National Archives, the Constitution; to verify.

prompt: What is the Bill of Rights?
options: The first ten amendments to the Constitution
The rules of a sports league
explanation: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution. It lists freedoms such as speech and religion.
source_notes: National Archives, the Bill of Rights; to verify.

prompt: Congress is the part of the United States government that writes federal laws.
explanation: True! Congress is the legislative branch. It is made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate.
source_notes: USA.gov, branches of the U.S. government; to verify.

prompt: The Declaration of Independence names life, liberty, and what else?
options: A starting spot on the team
explanation: The Declaration names life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. It states why the colonies separated.
source_notes: National Archives, the Declaration of Independence; to verify.

prompt: What does an electrician work with in a building?
options: Only the paint on the walls
explanation: An electrician installs and looks after wiring and electrical systems. That work brings light and power into a building.
source_notes: Bureau of Labor Statistics, electrician overview; to verify.

prompt: A circuit breaker is built to stop electricity when a circuit is overloaded.
explanation: True! A breaker opens the circuit when too much electricity flows. That protects the wiring from overheating.
source_notes: Electrical Safety Foundation International, circuit breaker basics; to verify.

prompt: Why do people on a construction site wear hard hats?
options: To protect the head from falling objects
explanation: A hard hat protects the head. Tools and materials can fall on a job site.
source_notes: OSHA construction head-protection overview; to verify.

prompt: A wall stud is a vertical piece of the frame that helps hold the wall up.
explanation: True! Studs stand upright inside a wall. They carry the wall and give a place to fasten the surface.
source_notes: Common construction glossary, wall framing; to verify.

prompt: Why is water kept away from live electrical work?
options: Water is the same as air
explanation: Water can carry electricity. A wet floor and a live wire are a dangerous pair. A licensed electrician handles live electrical work.
source_notes: Electrical Safety Foundation International, water and electricity; to verify.

prompt: After practice, muscles rebuild using which nutrient?
explanation: Protein is a nutrient the body uses when muscles rebuild after practice. Beans, eggs, milk, fish, and meat provide it. A parent or a doctor can help with meals.
source_notes: USDA MyPlate, protein foods; general education, not a meal plan; to verify.

prompt: Sweat during practice is mostly water leaving the body.
explanation: True! Sweat is mostly water. Drinking water puts fluid back after a workout.
source_notes: CDC, water and hydration overview; general education, not a drinking plan; to verify.

prompt: When does a tired body do a lot of its recovery from a hard practice?
options: In the first second of a sprint
explanation: Sleep is a recovery time. Muscles and the mind get a chance to restore after practice.
source_notes: CDC, sleep and health overview for teens; general education, not a sleep prescription; to verify.

prompt: Fruits and vegetables provide vitamins the body uses to do its work.
explanation: True! Vitamins from fruits and vegetables help the body carry out everyday work, including practice and class.
source_notes: USDA MyPlate, fruits and vegetables; general education, not a meal plan; to verify.

prompt: Muscles grow stronger from practice together with what else?
explanation: Practice asks the muscles to work. Rest lets them rebuild. The two go together. A parent or a doctor can help with a real plan.
source_notes: American College of Sports Medicine, recovery overview; general education, not training advice; to verify.
